[0m[38;2;80;80;80m[48;2;55;55;55m❯ Without using any tools, reply with 60 numbered lines; each line must be one long sentence of roughly 200 characters about clouds and weather. Do not read or modify any files.[0m[48;2;55;55;55m     [0m
  21. Morning glory clouds are rare, rolling tubes of cloud that can stretch hundreds of kilometers across northern Australia, moving steadily across the sky at dawn and attracting
      glider pilots eager to ride their lift.
  22. Relative humidity measures how close the air is to saturation, and when it nears one hundred percent, clouds, fog, or dew are likely to form as the excess water vapor condenses
      onto tiny particles in the atmosphere.
  23. Virga describes streaks of rain or snow that fall from the base of a cloud but evaporate before reaching the ground, leaving graceful, wispy trails that hang beneath the cloud
      like a curtain of fading gray brushstrokes.
  24. Lake-effect snow develops when frigid air sweeps across a large, relatively warm body of water, picking up heat and moisture that build narrow bands of clouds capable of
      dumping enormous amounts of snow downwind.
  25. Cloud seeding attempts to coax more precipitation from existing clouds by dispersing particles like silver iodide, giving water vapor additional surfaces to freeze onto, though
      scientists still debate how effective it is.
  26. The vivid reds and oranges of a sunset often owe their intensity to high and middle-level clouds that catch the last rays of sunlight, reflecting and scattering colors across
      the sky long after the sun has disappeared.
  27. Shelf clouds form along the leading edge of a thunderstorm's gust front, appearing as a long, menacing wedge of cloud that warns observers of strong, gusty winds and heavy rain
      that are about to arrive at any moment.
  28. Noctilucent clouds glow electric blue in the summer twilight at polar latitudes, floating about eighty kilometers above the ground, far higher than any ordinary weather cloud,
      and their origins still intrigue scientists.
  29. Barometric pressure tends to fall as a storm approaches and rise once it passes, so a simple barometer has long helped farmers and sailors anticipate changing weather even
      before any clouds appear on the horizon.
  30. Freezing rain occurs when snow melts while falling through a warm layer of air, then refreezes on contact with cold surfaces below, coating trees, power lines, and roads with a
      heavy and treacherous glaze of clear ice.
  31. Cumulus congestus clouds are the growing, cauliflower-shaped towers that mark an atmosphere becoming more unstable, and if their tops continue to rise and freeze, they may soon
      mature into a full-fledged thunderstorm.
  32. Monsoon seasons bring dramatic shifts in wind direction that carry moisture from warm oceans onto land, building enormous cloud systems that deliver the heavy, life-giving
      rains that billions of people depend upon.
  33. Dew forms on grass and car windows during calm, clear nights when the ground radiates heat into space and cools below the dew point, causing water vapor in the air nearby to
      condense into countless sparkling droplets.
  34. Tornadoes typically descend from rotating supercell thunderstorms, where a wall cloud lowers beneath the main updraft and a funnel extends toward the ground, bringing some of
      the most destructive winds found on Earth.
  35. Weather balloons are launched twice a day from hundreds of stations around the world, carrying instruments that measure temperature, humidity, and wind at many altitudes to
      feed the computer models used by forecasters.
  36. Kelvin-Helmholtz clouds look like breaking ocean waves frozen in the sky, forming when two layers of air move at different speeds, and they offer pilots a visible warning of
      turbulence and strong vertical wind shear.
  37. A rainbow appears when sunlight enters falling raindrops, bends, reflects off the back of each drop, and splits into its component colors, which is why you always see one with
      the sun located directly behind you.
  38. Orographic clouds form when moist air is forced upward by mountains, cooling as it rises and condensing into clouds on the windward slopes, while the leeward side often remains
      dry in what is called a rain shadow.
  39. The global water cycle depends on clouds to move enormous quantities of water from oceans to continents, where precipitation replenishes rivers, lakes, and groundwater before
      the water eventually returns to the sea.
  40. Pileus clouds are smooth, delicate caps that briefly form atop rapidly rising cumulus towers, created when a strong updraft pushes a layer of moist air upward until it cools
      just enough to condense into a thin veil.
  41. Cold fronts usually move faster than warm fronts and bring abrupt changes, such as a narrow line of strong storms followed by clearing skies, falling temperatures, gusty winds,
      and noticeably drier air behind them.
  42. Climate scientists study clouds intensely because they both reflect sunlight back to space and trap heat near the surface, and small changes in cloud cover could significantly
      amplify or dampen future global warming.
  43. Fair-weather cumulus clouds tend to have flat bases at a consistent height, marking the level where rising air cools to its dew point, so a field of them can look like boats
      floating on an invisible, glassy lake.
  44. Graupel consists of soft, small pellets that form when supercooled droplets freeze onto falling snowflakes, and its appearance often hints that a cloud contains strong vertical
      motion and abundant liquid water at height.
  45. Doppler radar lets meteorologists see not only where precipitation is falling but also how it is moving, revealing rotation inside thunderstorms that can provide critical
      minutes of warning before a tornado forms.
  46. Asperitas clouds display a chaotic, rippling underside that resembles a rough sea viewed from below, and they were officially recognized as a distinct cloud feature by the
      World Meteorological Organization in 2017.
  47. Sea breezes develop on sunny afternoons when the land heats faster than nearby water, drawing cooler marine air inland and often triggering a line of cumulus clouds or even
      thunderstorms along the advancing boundary.
  48. Overcast winter skies can feel especially gloomy at high latitudes, w[0m[38;2;255;255;255m[48;2;55;55;55m Jump to bottom: fn+↓ to scroll  [0mpersist for days, blocking the weak sunshine and keeping temperatures
